vignettes.stem: A wound swab grows gram-positive cocci in clusters. The colonies are golden and beta-hemolytic on blood agar, and the isolate is catalase positive. Which additional result best identifies the organism as Staphylococcus aureus?

options.explanation: Wrong: catalase positivity already places the isolate with the staphylococci, and streptococci are the catalase-negative group. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S2]]
Wrong: a coagulase-negative result points to a staphylococcus other than S. aureus. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S2]]
Correct: coagulase positivity separates S. aureus from most other staphylococci. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S2]]
Wrong: chains suggest a streptococcus; the stem describes clusters, a staphylococcal arrangement. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S2]]

options.text: Alpha-hemolysis with a green zone on blood agar
options.explanation: Wrong: the stem gives beta-hemolytic golden colonies, the S. aureus pattern, not a green alpha-hemolytic zone. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S2]]

vignettes.stem: A researcher studies why S. aureus survives in blood despite circulating antibodies. Mutants lacking one surface protein are cleared much faster because antibody-coated bacteria are phagocytosed. Which factor was deleted?

options.explanation: Wrong: the polysaccharide capsule resists phagocytosis directly; it does not bind the antibody Fc region. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S3]]
Correct: protein A binds the Fc region of IgG, blocking opsonization and phagocytosis. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S3]]
Wrong: clumping factor binds fibrinogen and does not act on IgG. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S3]]
Wrong: TSST-1 is a secreted superantigen that drives cytokine release, not a surface protein that blocks opsonization. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S4]]
Wrong: PVL is a secreted toxin that kills leukocytes; it does not bind IgG. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S4]]

vignettes.stem: A young adult develops sudden high fever, hypotension, a diffuse sunburn-like rash, and vomiting in the days after a surgical wound packing procedure. Wound culture grows S. aureus. Which virulence factor best explains the shock?

options.text: TSST-1, a superantigen that cross-links MHC II and the T-cell receptor
options.explanation: Correct: TSST-1 acts outside the peptide groove and causes massive cytokine release, producing toxic shock syndrome. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S4]]
Wrong: exfoliative toxins cause staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, with skin blistering rather than shock. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S4]]
Wrong: preformed enterotoxins cause rapid-onset vomiting after a meal, not a multisystem shock picture. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S4]]
Wrong: PVL kills leukocytes and is linked to necrotizing skin infection and pneumonia. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S4]]
Wrong: protein A blocks opsonization on the bacterial surface and is not a superantigen. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S3]]

vignettes.stem: A person who injects drugs presents with fever and a new regurgitant murmur. Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in clusters that are coagulase positive. Which valve is most often involved in this setting?

options.explanation: Wrong: the lecture ties endocarditis in people who inject drugs to the tricuspid valve, not the mitral valve. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S5]]
Wrong: the aortic valve is not the classic site in this setting; the lecture names the tricuspid valve. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S5]]
Wrong: the pulmonic valve is rarely the focus; the lecture names the tricuspid valve. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S5]]
Correct: S. aureus endocarditis is often tricuspid in people who inject drugs. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S5]]

options.text: No valve is typically involved; infection stays in the skin
options.explanation: Wrong: invasive disease includes bacteremia and endocarditis, beyond skin and soft tissue infection. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S5]]

vignettes.stem: A skin abscess fails to improve on a beta-lactam. Culture grows S. aureus that carries mecA on a mobile element. What explains the treatment failure?

options.text: Protein A binds the Fc region of IgG
options.explanation: Wrong: protein A impairs opsonization; it does not make the organism resistant to beta-lactam drugs. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S3]]
Wrong: PVL is a virulence toxin and does not explain drug resistance. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S4]]
Wrong: coagulase is a lab identification marker and is unrelated to beta-lactam resistance. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S2]]
Wrong: the capsule affects immune evasion, not antibiotic target binding. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S3]]

options.text: PBP2a, encoded by mecA, has low affinity for beta-lactams
options.explanation: Correct: mecA on the SCCmec element encodes PBP2a, giving resistance to almost all beta-lactams. [[MICRO/Staphylococcus aureus (sample lecture)#S6]]
